items.example_en: Hi, how's it going?
items.note: The h is always silent in Spanish.

items.example_en: Good morning, how can I help you?
items.note: Plural in Spanish. Switches to buenas tardes after lunch.

items.example: Buenas tardes, una mesa para dos.
items.example_en: Good afternoon, a table for two.
items.note: Used from after lunch until dark, then buenas noches.

items.example_en: Hi! How was the weekend?
items.note: Opening and closing question marks are obligatory in writing.

items.example_en: Good morning, how are you?
items.note: usted takes third-person verb forms, which trips up every beginner.

items.example_en: Nice to meet you, I'm Ana.
items.note: Encantado (m) or encantada (f) works just as well.

items.example_en: A coffee, please.
Thank you very much for your help.
Thanks. You're welcome.
items.note: In Latin America you will also hear con gusto or no hay de qué.

items.example_en: Excuse me, where is the exit?
items.note: Informal: perdona. Use it to get attention.

items.example_en: I'm sorry, I'm late.
items.note: A real apology; perdón is the lighter bump-into-you version.

items.example_en: Excuse me, I'm coming through.
items.note: Said when squeezing past someone or leaving a table.

items.example_en: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.
I'm off now, see you later!
items.note: The default casual goodbye in Spain, even for people you will never see again.

items.example_en: Sorry, I don't understand well.
items.note: entender is a stem-changing verb: e becomes ie when stressed.

items.example_en: Can you repeat more slowly, please?
How do you say window in Spanish?
items.note: The impersonal se: how does one say it.

items.example: Hablo un poco de español, pero despacio.
items.example_en: I speak a little Spanish, but slowly.
items.note: Said early, it makes everyone slow down for you.

items.example_en: My name is Stijn, and you?
items.note: Literally I call myself: a reflexive verb.

items.example_en: Hi, what's your name?
items.note: Formal: ¿cómo se llama usted?

items.example: Soy belga, pero vivo en España.
items.example_en: I'm Belgian, but I live in Spain.
items.note: Nationalities are lowercase and take no article after ser.

items.example_en: I'm from Ghent, in Belgium.
items.note: Origin is always ser, never estar.

items.example: Vivo en Valencia desde hace tres años.
items.example_en: I've lived in Valencia for three years.
items.note: desde hace plus a period covers the English present perfect.

items.example: Tengo treinta años y mi hermana veinte.
items.example_en: I'm thirty and my sister is twenty.
items.note: Spanish HAS years. Never soy treinta.

items.english: I work in, I work at
items.example_en: I work at a school.
I'm a biology student.
items.note: Professions drop the article after ser: soy médico, not soy un médico.

items.english: what do you do for a living?
items.example_en: And you, what do you do for a living?
items.note: The natural Spanish way to ask about someone's job.

items.example_en: I've been learning Spanish since January.
items.note: estar plus gerund: the action in progress. Origin uses ser, activity uses estar.

items.example: Me gusta mucho la música española.
items.example_en: I really like Spanish music.
items.note: Backwards from English: the thing liked is the subject, so plural means gustan.

items.example_en: Sorry, do you speak English?
items.note: Word order stays the same; only intonation and the marks change.

items.example_en: Three coffees, please.
items.note: uno becomes un before a masculine noun: un café.

items.example_en: That's ten euros in total.

items.example: El autobús sale en veinte minutos.
items.example_en: The bus leaves in twenty minutes.
items.note: 21 to 29 are written as one word: veintiuno, veintidós.

items.example_en: The ticket costs a hundred euros.
items.note: cien on its own, ciento when followed by more: ciento veinte.

items.example_en: It cost fifteen hundred euros.
items.note: Never un mil. Spanish uses a comma for decimals and a dot for thousands.

items.example_en: How much does this bag cost?
items.note: Plural things: ¿cuánto cuestan?

items.example_en: Sorry, what time is it?
It's a quarter past eight.
items.note: Plural son las, except one o'clock: es la una.

items.example: El tren sale a las diez y media.
items.example_en: The train leaves at half past ten.
items.note: menos cuarto is quarter to.

items.example: Corro por la mañana antes del trabajo.
items.example_en: I run in the morning before work.
items.note: With a clock time it switches to de: a las ocho de la mañana.

items.example_en: The weather is lovely today.
items.note: ayer is yesterday, mañana is tomorrow and also morning.

items.example_en: I'm going right now.
items.note: In Spain, ahora can also mean in a little while.

items.example_en: See you on Monday.
items.note: The article replaces English on. los lunes means every Monday.

items.example_en: What are you doing this weekend?
My birthday is in January.
items.note: Months are lowercase and take en.

items.example: Lo hablamos la semana que viene.
items.example_en: We'll talk about it next week.
items.note: Also la próxima semana. Last week is la semana pasada.

items.example: Las tiendas cierran el uno de mayo.
items.example_en: The shops close on the first of May.
items.note: Dates use plain numbers, not ordinals, in most of the Spanish-speaking world.

items.example_en: I always have breakfast at home.
items.note: Family: nunca, a veces, casi nunca, todos los días.
